The problem with lot of so called "Anti-War" movies is that they somehow glorify many elements of war via Protagonist, add heroism to it.

Kobayashi's Human Condition Trilogy made me realise it as it establishes there Nothing,absolutely nothing Heroic or Glorifying the war. The Protagonist is a humanist by core, a passionate member of the troops yet he sees no point in war and his faith is displayed by his final fate.

In order to establish an Anti-war film, you gotta take away all the Heroic stuff, verily from the hero himself.

I'd say This trilogy along with Come And See are the best anti-war films I've watched ever (from my 1350+ film watching experience in last 4 years)

I've been watching a lot of courtroom dramas recently, and something I've been trying to determine is: How much of the movie must take place in an actual courtroom for it to be considered a courtroom  drama?

Several I've seen recommended online have 1 or even no courtroom scenes. What are your opinions on this?

Going to finish Mahjong tonight and slightly sad that I won't have anymore "new" Edward Yang films to watch. I definitely need to rewatch Yi-Yi though as it was my first Yang film and I don't think I appreciated it enough on first watch.

It's a great film and one that certainly rewards rewatching.

What might come across (at first) as random, meandering slice of life reveals a strong structure in the constant parallels and contrasts between the three main characters' experiences.

Is there a particular film that gets labeled "courtroom drama" without courtroom scenes? 

I've also heard the term "legal drama," which perhaps includes but is not limited to courtroom dramas.

Yes, several people have listed these as courtroom dramas but have no courtroom scenes:

Dark Waters (2019)

The Firm (1993)

The Pelican Brief (1993)

I'm sure there are others but those 3 come to mind right away.

In my most recent post 2 of those movies were recommended as courtroom dramas. I consider them legal dramas like you mentioned.

Then some movies have less than 10 minutes of scenes in a courtroom but are considered courtroom dramas by several people. Including:

Erin Brockovich (2000)

The Mauritanian (2021)

The Client (1994)

I've tried searching in various places online and haven't seen much discussion on the distinction between courtroom dramas and legal dramas, and how much overlap there is.
Have you seen La Grande Illusion?

The American Film Institute published a list of their top 10 courtroom dramas and include In Cold Blood (1967). I just watched it and the only courtroom scene doesn't occur until 1hr 52min into the movie and it lasts less than 4 minutes. The rest of the movie is a police investigation/outlaws on a crime spree. 

It's a decent movie, but I wouldn't consider it a courtroom drama or even a legal drama. Just posting this to add to the discourse, not expecting an actual answer. I think it may just be a very loosely defined sub-genre. Ideally courtroom dramas would take place at least 70% in the courtroom but that's just my personal preference.

taking a tangent here, have you watched The Verdict (1982)? If yes, what are your thoughts on it? in my opinion it's one of the best courtroom dramas with 12 Angry Men and Anatomy Of A Murder.


Also do you consider To Kill A Mockingbird (1962) a courtroom drama? I personally don't

Yes, The Verdict is really good. I have it ranked at 12 for courtroom dramas. 12 Angry Men I have ranked at 4 and Anatomy of a Murder ranked at 11. Honestly the ranking of my top 12 could be rearranged in any order and I'd be okay with it. They're all so good.

I do consider To Kill a Mockingbird a courtroom drama but I can completely see why some wouldn't. I  just went back and fast forwarded through it to see how much of the movie actually takes place in a courtroom and it's just under 33 minutes. 

What confuses me is when a movie that spends less than 10 minutes in the courtroom is labeled a courtroom drama.

How is it that this sub has 500k members, yet only 1-2 posts and a handful of comments per day? 

In any case, last night I watched Goodbye, Dragon Inn, my first Tsai Ming-liang film. I simultaneously enjoyed it, but couldn't stop my mind from wandering most of the time; only the next cut would snap me out of my various daydreams. Nonetheless, the final scene hit me pretty hard and really summed up the impact of the preceding 80 minutes. A tough watch to get through at times but one that will certainly stick with me for a while.

Would love to discuss that film, if you're interested.

Have you ever seen the original *Dragon Inn*?

Hi, surely! 

I have not seen Dragon Inn, but I'm told it enhances GDI significantly. Maybe I'll have watched it by the time I revisit this. 

I'm not really sure why GDI was on my mind at all, but I heard about it a few months ago when browsing for more Taiwanese films. I've seen most of Edward Yang's films and loved all of them, so it was mostly him who sent me here. 

Not sure how much commentary I can really draw from GDI, but man what a gorgeous building that is. The idea of the "place that was once grand and bustling" is very appealing (ie The Grand Budapest Hotel), and I enjoyed the way that idea was explored here, only once giving us any glimpse of the setting at its height. The empty stairwells and hallways are so evocative of the mid-20th century and I think the lingering shots enhance the effect. I couldn't help but imagine all the people who have enjoyed that setting in the past, all of the first dates, family movie outings, birthday parties... it didn't make me cry, but it made me want to. 

I'm left with such a vivid conception of the theater that I feel like I can almost explore it in my head, as if I was a little kid who sneaked out of a showing to wander the halls. We see a lot of different rooms and angles, but then there are still more parts of it that we don't see- all the closed doors and shadowy corners. The cumulative effect is that we're trying to wrap our heads around an absolutely massive space- massive physically but also emotionally, culturally, imaginatively. So by the final scene, when we've left the theater forever and finally get the one piece of non-diegetic music in the film, it all comes at you like a ton of bricks. 

I'm gonna ignore the "microcosm of cinema's trajectory in the broader culture" side of this for now, partly because I'm still working through that and partly because I typed a lot here already. This is a good example of a film that I wasn't really enraptured by during the watch, but that still GAVE me a lot and will continue to do so for a while.

It's a really interesting film. It's been described as minimalistic and that's a good adjective -- there is so little movement in the frame that, when it does happen, it has a unique impact. And allows the film to have a powerful atmosphere of stillness and, ultimately, of death. 

Your third paragraph is spot-on, and I think gets at why you found the film somewhat opaque. Almost all the films we watch are ultimately about characters: their hopes, fears, desires, journeys. This is a film about a place. The theater itself is really the protagonist.

Re: Tsai Ming-liang, I'd highly recommend his debut film, *Rebels of the Neon God*, which has a more conventional plot but also captures the same atmosphere of rainy, urban Taiwanese anomie.

I actually *tried* to watch Rebels of the Neon God a few weeks back, but my go-to obscure film site didn't have subtitles on it. I'll give it another go soon for sure, I mean come on it has neon in the title, I'll obviously love it. 

I'd be curious to hear your thoughts about the two human "leads" here. I can appreciate how the ticket lady fits in here, but I'm more iffy on the japanese tourist. I've seen people say he was cruising, which I sort of missed while I was watching. He provides some good comedy (the bathroom scene is a comedic marvel), but thematically he seems like an odd type of patron to focus on.

What did you think of Mahjong? I'm thinking about watching it tonight or in the next few days. 

I've seen Yi Yi, Terrorizers, ABSD, and Taipei Story, with Yi Yi being my favorite. I heard that the comedies, Mahjong and Confucian Confusion, are a bit less accessible than the rest, but maybe I'm misremembering.

It's really worth a watch.

To answer your question, I think one potential answer is that this tourist (tourist being the quintessential outsiders) provides an interesting contrast to the movie theater as a communal space, as a gathering place for people in a specific neighborhood. That is of course the opposite of a tourist's perspective.

I'll admit I passed out early and didn't get to finish it lol. So, I'll hopefully remember to respond to this tomorrow. The first ~30 minutes have been great so far. Confucian Confusion was really good. Probably my least favorite of his works but I enjoyed them all so much that that doesn't mean much. I think ABSD was my favorite of them all, but that may change when I rewatch Yi-Yi.
Happens to the best of us!

I just finished it and I thoroughly enjoyed it. I'm hard-pressed to call either of them "comedies," at least from an American perspective of a comedy. But they definitely had a lot of funny moments compared to his other works. I'm glad I watched it though. Just don't expect anything on the level of Yi-Yi or ABSD, or even Taipei story or That Day, on the Beach. If you're a fan of Yang you'll probably enjoy it, but it was definitely not his best film.

This place is for true *scholars*, so most just read here.

It's either that or laziness.

I'm genuinely stoked Sean Baker won the Palme D'or for Anora. I've been a lifelong fan ever since Florida Project. I had a lot of time for Red Rocket, but I understand why it was seen as a misstep by some. I'm so pleased he's scoring big with this new film. I can't wait to see it.
Any thoughts on *Once Upon a Time in America*?

*Yi Yi* and *A Brighter Summer Day* are both truly great films. I prefer the former, myself, because it just hits me harder, emotionally. And I think it's possible the best cinematic representation of the joy and excitement of a new, promising, business partnership (and the disappointment when it falls through).

Have been flirting with wanting to blog for a bit, but I mostly never do it. Here is the link to a site I created 2 years ago where I've posted a whopping two reviews/essays. They are about Medicine For Melancholy, Barry Jenkins' first film and The Go-Between, a 1971 Joseph Losey film I watched last night for the first time.

I'd be willing to listen to feedback if you have any, so here it is (essentially no one has ever gone): [https://catchinguponculture.blogspot.com/](https://catchinguponculture.blogspot.com/)

I'm not trying to revolutionize review writing, but my original intent was to write about interesting generally older films (and sometimes other topics) and eventually do bigger essays regarding specific directors, eras, actors, etc.
